title: #stitch @BravoWWHL We love taxonomy on this page! #theatre #immersive...
transcript: so Patti LuPone was on her usual business of talking sh!t about Andrew Lloyd Webber when she accidentally said something really interesting that I wish more people knew about Andy Cohen asked her about Masquerade the immersive Phantom show and in the midst of talking about how unappealing it sounds to her she makes this throwaway comment: “it's like Promenade Theatre” “I don't know why they're calling it immersive” “unless it's there's movies of stuff, I don't know” the reason this caught my attention as a fan of immersive theatre is that the term “promenade” is very underutilized, in my opinion to the point where I'm guessing a lot of people haven't even heard it I don't think it's specifically a British term but I do think it's used more in the UK Patti is like one of the first American people I've seen use it but I've been saying for years that we should be adopting it more widely “promenade” essentially refers to a type of immersive theatre where the audience moves from location to location and you might be thinking “isn't that just what immersive theatre is?” and no not exclusively, that's the confusion here Sleep No More is a promenade show and it played a large role in introducing a lot of people to the concept of immersive theatre and I think a lot of those people myself included at the time just said “oh so this is what immersive theatre is” interestingly the word “promenade” was actually used on the official American Sleep No more website but it didn't really catch on Then, as immersive theatre became more trendy and popular a lot of theatre fans got confused when shows would market themselves as “immersive” even if the audience stayed in one place because we didn't have the word “promenade” to delineate them I just picked Comet as a random example here but I can't tell you how many shows there have been where I've heard people be like “well it's not really immersive” “because the audience doesn't move around like they do in Sleep No More” now on some level it's absolutely true that “immersive” has become an overused marketing buzzword but I think accusations of false advertising are a little unfair because they're using “immersive” as an adjective not as a label for the art form and I think that's fair game by now most of us have picked up on the fact that the word “immersive” can apply to a whole range of experiences but ironically we still haven't picked up the word “promenade” even though it would be very useful on both the marketing side and the consumer side to have that extra layer of specificity in our vocabulary now the part of Patti’s comment that confused me a little was when she said “I don't know why they're calling it immersive” “unless it's there's movies of stuff” if I had to guess she was probably thinking of stuff like this like the immersive Van Gogh experience Which sort of makes sense when you consider this is probably one of the more widely recognizable examples of an immersive experience, like for the general public extending beyond the theatre bubble but considering she's very much in the theatre bubble I'm a little surprised this is where her mind went first but I'm not sure what else she would have meant by the screens in any case Patti was wrong in the sense that Masquerade absolutely can be called “immersive” theatre but she was *right* in the sense that “promenade” is a more specific (and therefore I think more useful) term to describe it or at least it would be more useful if more people knew about it
